title: Sariputta and Moggallana
hookLine: Assaji's short verse: things arise from a cause, and the Buddha tells their cause; Sariputta understands at once

cards: Two best friends make a pact: whoever finds the answer first tells the other. Upatissa and Kolita grew up together, sons of important families near the city of Rajagaha.
As young men they went to a festival, looked at the crowds laughing and the actors on stage, and both thought the same thing: in a hundred years, none of these people will be alive.

So they left home together to search for what doesn't die. They studied with a well-known teacher, learned everything he had, and it wasn't enough. Then one morning in Rajagaha, Upatissa sees a monk walking for alms.

teach.b: The monk is Assaji, one of the five from the Deer Park. What catches Upatissa's eye is the way he walks: calm, collected, eyes down, every movement settled.
Upatissa follows him, waits politely until he's finished his meal, and asks: who is your teacher, and what does he teach? Assaji is honest. I'm new, he says.

teach.h: I CAN ONLY GIVE THE GIST.
teach.b: I can't explain the teaching at length, but I can tell you the gist. And he says a single verse, four short lines. In paraphrase: of things that arise from a cause, the Buddha has told the cause, and also how they cease.

That's the teaching of the great one. Hearing it, the texts say, Upatissa's dhamma eye opened, the same clear seeing Kondañña had: whatever arises, ceases. He runs to Kolita, who sees his face and knows at once.
Did you find it? Upatissa repeats the verse, and Kolita understands too.
The pact is kept. They go to the Buddha together, with many of their old teacher's students. Upatissa becomes known as Sariputta, son of Sari, his mother's name.
Kolita becomes Moggallana. They become the Buddha's two chief disciples, Sariputta known for wisdom, Moggallana for deep meditation powers.
That little verse, in Pali ye dhamma hetuppabhava, became one of the most copied lines in the Buddhist world.
It's been found carved on stones, stamped on clay seals, and set inside statues and stupas across Asia, as a summary of the whole teaching.
The Dhammapada says one word of sense, which brings peace to the hearer, is better than a thousand empty ones.

how: Sariputta and Moggallana are honored as the Buddha's two chief disciples, often shown standing on either side of him in temples, and Assaji's verse, 'ye dhamma hetuppabhava', is still chanted and has been inscribed on stupas, seals and images across Asia.

o: the monk who gave the verse in the street
the chief disciple known for his wisdom
the Buddha's cousin and lifelong attendant

games.q: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.
p: gave the verse, one of the five

s: Assaji gave a long, detailed explanation
he said he was new and could only give the gist: one short verse.
Sariputta was first drawn by the way Assaji walked
Assaji's verse has been found inscribed across Asia
on stones, clay seals, statues and stupas.

games.q: you're Upatissa. you've just heard the verse that changed everything. what do you do first?
o: stay with Assaji and ask for more.
go straight to the Buddha alone.
run to tell your friend Kolita.
games.why: he keeps the pact and runs to Kolita, who reads it in his face, hears the verse, and understands too.

practice: Think back over what's helped you, here or anywhere: a saying, a verse, a sentence someone said at the right moment, and pick just one. Say it silently a few times, and feel why it helped.
Then picture one person who might need it, and hold just the line for them, no lecture, the way Assaji gave it.

wordCard.voice: Sariputta. One of two friends who kept their pact, and became the Buddha's chief disciples, after hearing one short verse from the monk Assaji.

orig.note: Pali: 'those things that arise from a cause', the first line of Assaji's verse.

carryVoice: Your line: one verse was enough. Four short lines, and two friends kept their pact. Sixty-eight days now.
